title: MEDI2004 W1 · Introduction to Pharmacology
subject: Pharmacology Fundamentals
content: Drug = any substance producing a biological effect when administered (synthetic, natural, or genetically engineered). Endogenous substances aren't drugs unless administered (own insulin = hormone; injected = drug). Drug = active chemical; medicine = drug + excipients in a dose form (medicine contains the drug); drug class = drugs sharing mechanism/target/therapeutic use. Vitamins/herbs act as drugs when they produce effects (label doesn't decide). Pharmacology = study of drugs and their interactions with living systems; branches: pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, pharmacotherapeutics, toxicology, pharmacogenetics, clinical pharmacology. PK = body->drug (ADME; sets dose/timing); PD = drug->body (mechanism/effect; sets effect & side effects). Classes: analgesic (pain), anaesthetic (removes sensation), anxiolytic (anxiety), sedative (sleep), stimulant (CNS activity), antidepressant (SSRIs), antipsychotic, antihypertensive (ACE inhibitors), antineoplastic (cancer), anabolic steroid, hallucinogen, PrEP (HIV prevention). Prefixes: anti- = against, -lytic = relieves/breaks, an-/anaes- = without.

questions.question: In pharmacology, a drug is best defined as any substance that:
options: A. produces a biological effect when administered
B. is manufactured only in a laboratory
C. requires a doctor's prescription to obtain
D. is formulated into a tablet form
questions.explanation: A drug is any substance producing a biological effect when given to a living organism, regardless of source, prescription status or dose form.

questions.question: The body's own insulin is a hormone, but injected insulin is a drug because it is:
options: A. administered from outside the body
B. chemically different from natural insulin
D. present at very low concentrations
questions.explanation: A substance the body makes itself counts as a drug only when it is administered; the same molecule given from outside becomes a drug.

questions.question: Penicillin, obtained from a mould, is an example of a drug derived from:
questions.explanation: Penicillin is a natural chemical produced by a mould — a microorganism. Synthetic drugs are lab-made and biologics come from genetic engineering.

questions.question: What distinguishes a medicine from a drug?
options: A. a medicine is a drug plus excipients
B. a drug is a formulated therapeutic product
C. a medicine has no active chemical
D. a drug always contains several medicines
questions.explanation: A medicine is a drug formulated for therapeutic use — the active drug plus excipients in a dose form. The medicine contains the drug, not the reverse.

questions.question: A drug class groups together drugs that share a:
options: A. mechanism, target or therapeutic use
B. one shared chemical parent structure
C. one common manufacturing process step
D. a single route of administration
questions.explanation: Classes are grouped by shared mechanism, molecular target or therapeutic use — not by chemical family, how they're made, or route.

questions.question: Which question does pharmacokinetics answer?
options: A. what the body does to the drug
B. what the drug does to the body
C. how the drug binds its receptor
D. how the drug produces side effects
questions.explanation: Pharmacokinetics is body→drug (ADME): how the drug is handled. What the drug does to the body — receptor binding and effects — is pharmacodynamics.

questions.question: A change in a drug's ADME handling would most directly alter its:
questions.explanation: PK (ADME) mostly sets how much drug is present and when — the dose and timing. Receptor affinity, mechanism and target are pharmacodynamic properties.

questions.question: Which branch of pharmacology studies the harmful effects of chemicals and drugs?
questions.explanation: Toxicology addresses harmful effects. Pharmacogenetics studies genetic variation in response; pharmacotherapeutics the use of drugs to treat disease.

questions.question: The study of how genetic differences change drug response is called:
questions.explanation: Pharmacogenetics links inherited variation to differences in drug response. Clinical pharmacology is drug use in real patients more broadly.

questions.question: By the pharmacological definition, when is a high-dose vitamin considered a drug?
options: A. when it produces a biological effect
B. when it is labelled a supplement
C. when it is from a natural source
D. when it is taken with food
questions.explanation: The definition turns on effect, not the label: at pharmacological doses a vitamin produces drug-like effects, so it acts as a drug however it is marketed.

questions.question: A drug whose class is 'analgesic' primarily acts to:
questions.explanation: Analgesics relieve pain (e.g. paracetamol, morphine). Reducing anxiety is anxiolytic; lowering blood pressure is antihypertensive.

questions.question: The suffix '-lytic' in 'anxiolytic' indicates a drug that:
options: A. relieves or breaks something down
questions.explanation: '-lytic/-olytic' means breaks or relieves, so an anxiolytic relieves anxiety. 'anti-' means against; 'an-/anaes-' means without.

questions.question: Reading the name alone, an 'antineoplastic' drug acts against:
questions.explanation: 'anti-' means against and 'neoplastic' refers to new growths, so antineoplastics act against tumours (cytotoxic chemotherapy).

questions.question: Drugs in the 'anaesthetic' class are characterised by:
options: C. promoting tissue and muscle growth
questions.explanation: The 'an-/anaes-' root means without: anaesthetics remove sensation or consciousness. Stimulants raise CNS activity; anabolic steroids build tissue.

questions.question: Two patients given an identical dose reach very different blood levels. This is best explained by differing:
options: C. receptor densities in the patients
D. drug mechanisms in the patients
questions.explanation: Different blood levels from the same dose reflect how each body handles the drug — pharmacokinetics. Differences in effect at one level would be pharmacodynamic.

questions.question: The same blood concentration gives a strong effect in one patient and little in another. This reflects differences in:
questions.explanation: When effect differs at an identical concentration, the variation lies in how the drug acts on the body — pharmacodynamics. Absorption and excretion are PK.

questions.question: Caffeine and amphetamine belong to which drug class?
questions.explanation: Stimulants increase CNS activity. Sedatives calm and promote sleep — the opposite direction of effect.

questions.question: An ACE inhibitor used to lower blood pressure belongs to which class?
questions.explanation: 'anti-' + hypertension: antihypertensives lower blood pressure. The other 'anti-' classes target tumours, depression and psychosis.

questions.question: Pharmacology is best described as the study of:
options: A. how drugs interact with living systems
B. how medicines are manufactured in industry
C. how diseases are diagnosed in clinics
D. how medicines are stored and dispensed
questions.explanation: Pharmacology studies drugs and their interactions with living systems — spanning how drugs act and how the body handles them.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between a drug and a medicine?
options: A. a medicine contains a drug
B. a drug contains a medicine
C. they are identical in meaning
D. a drug excludes any excipients
questions.explanation: A medicine is the drug plus excipients in a dose form, so the medicine contains the drug. The terms are not interchangeable.

questions.question: A drug taken as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is used to:
questions.explanation: PrEP is pre-exposure prophylaxis — taken before potential exposure to prevent HIV infection, not to treat established disease.

questions.question: Which pair of drug classes have opposite effects on CNS activity?
questions.explanation: Sedatives calm and promote sleep while stimulants increase CNS activity — directly opposing effects. The other pairs don't oppose in that way.

questions.question: The shift from 'magical remedies' to modern pharmacology is best marked by drugs that are:
options: A. tested for proven effect and safety
B. derived only from natural plant sources
C. sold without any formal safety testing
D. based purely on tradition and belief
questions.explanation: Modern pharmacology rests on purified or synthesised drugs tested for evidence of effect and safety — the break from unregulated traditional remedies.

questions.question: Fluoxetine, an SSRI, is an example of which drug class?
questions.explanation: SSRIs such as fluoxetine treat depression and are antidepressants. Antipsychotics treat psychosis; anxiolytics reduce anxiety.

questions.question: Which branch specifically concerns drug use and effects in real patients?
questions.explanation: Clinical pharmacology studies how drugs behave and are used in actual patients. Pharmacotherapeutics is the use of drugs to treat disease more generally.

questions.question: To correct a problem caused purely by a drug's pharmacokinetics, the most logical adjustment is to:
options: A. change the dose or schedule
B. switch to a different receptor
D. select a new molecular target
questions.explanation: PK problems are about how much drug is present and when, so adjusting dose or timing addresses them; changing target or mechanism addresses PD issues.
